lessons.title: What literary texts are and how to read them
lessons.html:
What literary texts are

A literary text is a piece of writing or speaking made to tell a story, share feelings or ideas, and make us think. It is different from a work text like a job card or a safety notice, which only gives information.

Kinds of literary texts

  • Short stories and novels: stories about people (characters) and what happens to them.
  • Poems: short texts with lines, sounds and pictures in words.
  • Praise poetry (for example izibongo or lithoko): poems that honour a person, a clan or a leader.
  • Folktales: old stories told by elders, often with animals like the hare or jackal, that teach a lesson.
  • Songs: work songs, church songs, struggle songs.
  • Drama: plays acted out, on stage or radio.

The parts of a story

  • Characters: the people or animals in the story.
  • Setting: where and when it happens, for example a farm in the Karoo during a drought.
  • Plot: what happens, from the start, through the problem, to the end.
  • Conflict: the problem or struggle.
  • Theme: the big idea or lesson, for example hard work, greed, family, or respect for the land.

How to read a literary text

  1. Look at the title. What do you think the text is about?
  2. Read it once all the way through, for the feeling.
  3. Read it again slowly. Note words you do not know and work them out from the words around them.
  4. Ask: Who? Where? What happened? Why?
  5. Ask: How did it make me feel? Why?

There is often more than one good answer. What matters is that you can show where in the text your idea comes from.

lessons.title: Responding to a literary text
lessons.html:
Responding to a literary text

To respond means to give your thoughts and feelings about the text, and to explain them. You can respond by talking, writing or even acting.

A short poem to practise with

The rain came late this year,
the veld lay brown and still.
My father watched the empty sky
and fed the cows on hope until
one night the thunder spoke our name,
and morning smelled of earth again.

Questions to think about

  • What is the setting? (A farm in a dry season.)
  • Who is in the poem? (The speaker and the father.)
  • What does fed the cows on hope mean? The father had no feed left, only hope. This is a picture in words, not real food.
  • What does the thunder spoke our name mean? The rain came at last, as if it came for this family. The poet gives the thunder a human voice.
  • How does the poem make you feel? Worried at first, then happy and relieved.
  • What is the theme? Hope and patience in hard times.

Language tools writers use

  • Comparison: saying one thing is like another, for example the dust rose like smoke.
  • Giving human actions to things: the thunder spoke.
  • Repeating words or sounds to make them stand out.
  • Strong describing words that let you see, hear and smell the scene.

Giving your response

  1. Say what the text is about in one or two sentences.
  2. Give your opinion: did you like it, and why?
  3. Give a reason from the text: quote a line or describe a part.
  4. Link it to your own life, for example a dry year on your farm.
  5. Listen to others. They may see something different. Respect their view, and explain yours calmly.

Key points

  • Literary texts include stories, poems, praise poetry, folktales, songs and plays.
  • Stories have characters, setting, plot, conflict and theme.
  • Writers use pictures in words, comparisons and repetition.
  • A good response gives your opinion with a reason from the text.
  • Respect other readers' views.
